Who says this state wants low/unskilled labor.   Before computers were being built in this region, plenty of clothing was designed and built here (textiles are still heavily here).  This manufacturing long left this state in the late 80s/early 90s and there likely won't be any push to get most of that back.  The only major "plant" I'm aware of in this state is the electric vehicle one and I'm sure every representative will sign a blank check to the CEO to keep most of it in the state. This state has a very unique situation where we can attract all levels of skill.  Between our colleges and our companies, there is a heavy demand on highly skilled labor to design "things" -- there simply isn't a huge demand to build those "things".  So many other countries have already mastered the art of building, why does this state need it back? The big companies that have left include big car companies.  One left to the south -- not only for the low taxes, but because the manufacturing plants were already in that state (moving to that company also cut hundreds to thousands of jobs).  Another is moving their main HQ to a southern state, but none of their R&D.  They will also likely lose ~30-50% of their work force by moving (contractors to full time is nearly 2:1, they won't move any contractors).  Between the tax savings of simply getting out of this state, the tax breaks that the southern state will give and the sheer number of people that won't relocate (several of my neighbors work at that company, they aren't going), you're looking at massive savings by simply changing their PO. What I'm trying to say is: looking strictly at companies leaving this state for that southern state is a misnomer.  You need to dig into the details as to why these companies are leaving and understand that its not JUST lower wages and tax breaks.

> Of course it does, indirectly, that all trickles down. This has been an economic plan since the 80s and it has been proven that it doesn't work. > You start taking large numbers of incomes out of this state and you'll start seeing demand falling across the various markets, lessening the various resource demands, including unskilled labor.  You're actually listing something that residents *should* want: get more people to leave the state.  People leaving from the state (specifically in congested major cities) would increase the number of available houses.  With a surplus of housing, rents would have to be decreased to keep them filled.  The major city is very expensive, with no plans to build vertically and we lack affordable housing.  Getting enough people to move out of the city would help reduce the costs for everyone, in the city. The numbers of jobs and people leaving from the state are in the four and maybe five figure range.  The state has a population of ~18 million people and it would have to take *many* more people to leave the state before any changes were made for business taxes or incentives.  Giving companies a tax break once will make them threaten to do it again -- you have to accept that if they want to move, they *will* move.

Demand does it all -- it's Econ 101. Increasing the minimum will put more money into the pockets of people.  More money in their pockets (that isn't offset with higher expenses) will give them more money to spend.   > Shouldn't the average wage be higher than the current minimum if the demand were already there? If not, I would think that raising would only lessen demand and create a surplus of workers. The average wage *is* higher than the minimum, it's part of the definition differences between minimum and average.  You're looking at the raise in minimum wage purely from a business perspective.   Think about the situation if you're in the shoes of someone making the minimum -- you have MORE to spend.  YOU create a higher demand, NOT the business.  Now that YOU are demanding more of something, businesses will try to cater to your demands.  If one businesses can't handle the demand, more will follow. Let's also remember that the minimum wages is for the city and for businesses with >=25 people.  If you opened a taco restaurant (we can always use more) and are employing 25 people, your business sounds like it's healthy and thriving.  Mom and pop shops that have less than 25 employees should be welcoming this sort of increase, as now they can have new customers available because there will be more demand. > but I thought an increased number of businesses is what creates the demand, then in turn pulling up the wage. The opposite is actually true.  Businesses satisfy a demand.  If there are lots of businesses in the area, what's stopping them from lowering the wages?  You increase wages because you have to hire people to supply demand.  If you're over saturated in the ability to supply the demand, you don't need to pay high wages anymore and can easily let people go. If you want to push your analogy in the other direction: why not open a high end wedding cake shop in the middle of the lowest income city?  You've now created business that can pay good wages (as your prices are high), but there isn't any demand in the area for your cakes with the high cost.  It would make no economical sense for this, but that's where your analogy can go. (all analogies pushed to their extreme will fail)

As a user and owner of these, I can emphatically say that this will NOT be the future for all fighting games (let alone the series). These are things that are much easier for me to do on a touch interface: - Insta air things.  Specifically, things that don't have a height requirement. - Comboing into a character's special move.  Just spam the buttons and you're good to go. - Charge motions. - QCF/HCF and dashing feel "faster".  ymmv. - FADC things *are* faster, but I haven't quite mastered the timing for it. - 360 motions are great!  It's a three button pressing: F, B, D+U+attack.  Once you learn the timing on this, feels sneaky. Things not so bueno: - Tiring.  After an hour or so, my left hand is definitely tired.  I've played many hours at a time, but I'm simply not as comfy with it, compared to a stick.  Potentially a "lefty" version would play better for me, not sure. - SRK motions don't feel as fast.  You can go F,D,F+P on the touch interface, but it feels slower than a 'stick with the "wiggle" motion.  The shortcut can be helpful, but it's also tiring to hold down a button and then double tapping. - 720 motions are 100% difficult.  Yes, I've watch the tutorial.  Yes, I've put practice into this motion.  I simply can't. - "Zig zag" motions (guile/blank ultra/super) are a little difficult than a stick.  While I can do them on both sides, I definitely prefer it on a 'stick. There are a few characters I feel GREAT with playing and a few that I 100% avoid (typically grapplers that need/have a 720 motion).  Then there are characters I like to play, but are simply tiring to play with (divekick and charge characters, specifically). In addition to what I posted above, the engine doesn't handle touch interfaces all too well: - There is a lot of height restriction on moves, so you're not going to insta air everything.  A specific character's move is a terrible move, but the insta air makes it viable -- shame it has a height restriction. - Leniency on inputs can still cause moves you don't want to come out. While I *like* the controller, there are definitely trade offs.  Some have adapted very well to using one and I've given nearly 2+ years of using it on a weekly basis to understand my own limitations.

Comparing Windows' install to a linux install is a completely different world of design goals. > Locked to a tiny resolution With the sheer multitude of graphic cards available in the world, choosing 640x480 for just the install isn't a big deal.  Windows' goal is to quickly get you into the desktop and having some native resolution isn't going of any real benefit. > Bundles absolutely no software but the install script itself What do you even mean here?  Operating systems involve managing things like userland, network stack, storage, etc.  Window installs several pieces of software that are incredibly useful: Internet Explorer (how else am I going to download Chrome?), notepad, cmd.exe, etc.  Most of the linux installers I deal with install next to nothing on boot and I have to go get them once the OS is installed and network has started. > Lacks drivers upon the first boot What drivers are you talking about?  Are you talking a high end storage card?  Video?  Sound?  Networking?  I can give you several examples where a stock install won't find specific pieces of equipment.   All most want with a Windows install is to find the networking card -- so we can finish up whatever is left. > Awful partition utility (although you can get by with shift+F10 and diskpart) Windows Vista+ installer allows you to create several partitions off individual drives without needing diskpart.  What specific partitioning needs do you have that aren't feasible under Windows' GUI install?   Remember: Windows' goal is to get onto your drive and be your primary OS.  If you have needs beyond this, you simply need to plan accordingly. > Buggy as hell! Windows 7 has failed to install on any machine with at least one SSD and one HDD I've tried. It also randomly fails if you plug it into a USB 3 slot. Out of the tens of millions of Windows' installs, there aren't nearly this many instances where it will fail.  Windows will NOT install onto USB drives, it will only accept a drive that doesn't appear removable (a design decision kept since the early days of Windows).  Windows will never easily be installed onto a bootable drive (can be done, but with a lot of work) and this is well documented. Linux is meant to fit into so many different needs and roles -- that's why it's install is significantly more flexible.  Windows is meant to be your primary OS and will play nice ... when possible.

> So now artists get to happily go back to being paid next to nothing for their work What do *you* define as proper compensation for an artists work?  The RIAA and labels have their own definition, to which plenty of artists have agreed to those terms. Every song out there has a myriad of pieces that need to get paid: 1. Studio time. 2. Producers. 3. Mixers. 4. Writers. 5. Performers (album and live are different, but we'll treat them the same in this argument). Independent artists have little funds to rent studio time, hire producers, mixers and may be the only one performing the music for any given track or album -- this is why they seek representation from labels for their work.  Once they have representation, they can ask for loans to hire out the necessary people to finish their recordings. Given all the people I listed, how much should a famous singer be making on her most recent single?  Clearly, she's performing on that track, check.  Did she write it?  Did she produce (fund) it?  Did she record it in her own studio?  Did she mix it?  How about the other musicians that played on that track ... where is their compensation?  If I'm looking at this correctly, the singer may "only" be 1/5th of the team it took to get that ONE single out to the masses. Before we even try to calculate how much her one performance is worth, let's also forget the 800lb gorilla in the room: marketing.  The singer's face, name and voice is all over the place!  Imagine if she wasn't a household name and still had this single -- it likely wouldn't be nearly as popular. Artists have a choice with their work.  Sign and they gain access to funds, marketing and a slew of resources to help bring their work to the masses.  Not sign and it will be entirely up to them (financially) to get their work out the the masses. Contracts with the labels have been WELL scrutinized for 30+ years, it's very difficult to hide anything in them (anymore).

Taxi's aren't the problem, it's the laws. If you're a taxi driver, you need to pay for a license to drive professionally.  In order to keep this license, you need specific and clear markings on your car, insurance, etc.  These are all mandated by the government, no real way to get around it.  This situation is no different in many places (the cost is very high in some cities). Ride-sharing services are providing a service that costs less because it skirts virtually *every* law that was put in place to protect consumers -- hence why it's cheaper than traditional taxi's.  What these services are doing is providing a transportation service that is better than traditional cabs.  It would take very little work (ihmo) for cabs to adopt a model where it was 10x easier to get a taxi to come to pick you up, they simply haven't adopted with the times.

> So ride-sharing is going against the customer protection by loopholing laws and you want taxis to do the same. Yes.  Ride-sharing is completely bypassing local laws designed around this business. > Seems a specific tier of ride-sharing is the shit tier service. That specific tier is the unlicensed driver service that is getting the ban hammer because it works with unlicensed services. I swing at around that speed and had a few long yard "bombs" yesterday. > If I have to sacrifice some distance for more control then I'll still come out ahead in the long run. Until you are absolutely dedicated to a workout routine to get your swing speeds much faster (we're talking very fast, which is crazy fast), the differences in the shaft are going to make nearly that much difference.  The most common thing from a shaft that isn't stiff enough are the ball going really high into the air with both slices and hooks.  You've indicated you're slicing the ball often, this indicates a path+face problem and not a shaft problem. >  Which from what I have found on other forums will be the result with a stiffer club. Is that information accurate? Golf is heavily about "feel".  If you don't like the "feel" of something, it gets in your head and your confidence goes to shit, making you perform poorly.  Having confidence in your equipment (aided by "feel") will make you perform better.  Many golfers prefer the "feel" of a stiffer club, but their performance could likely be better with a more flexible one instead (possibly with more weight in the shaft). What I'm saying to you is: at the swing speeds you're listing, the differences in those shafts won't make a dramatic difference.  It's probably better than you fix your path+face issues, as that's the real cause of your slice.

It's a chicken and egg problem... Publisher need to pay bills and will use all of their available ad space to fill it with ads. Ad networks want to pay as little as possible for impressions, as their pay outs to the owners of the ads are as little as possible. If we (the consumers) want a better reading experience, publishers need to start reducing all the bad ads they are showing.  The only way they will do that is by getting more money from the ad networks that provide the ads.  Since there is zero incentive for the ad networks to starting paying more for the same impressions, this will never happen. The best model (imho) that we'll move to is paying some subscription to a series of different sites (vs. one at a time) where ads either go away completely or are dramatically reduced.  Publishers get what they want (money) and now the available ad space is worth FAR more not only to the publishers, but to the ad networks and companies that want to be in those premium positions.
